questions.prompt: What does Snellman say about x raised to the 0 power (for nonzero x)?
choices: A It equals 0.
B It equals 1; but 0⁰ is left undetermined (“I don’t know”).
C It equals x.
D It is always undefined for every x.
questions.explain: Nonzero bases to the 0 power give 1; he refuses to assign a value to 0⁰.

questions.prompt: When multiplying powers with the same base, what rule does Snellman emphasize?
choices: A Multiply the exponents and add the bases.
B Add the exponents (same base).
C Subtract the bases and ignore exponents.
D Divide the exponents.
questions.explain: Moral of the story: same base, multiply → add exponents (e.g., 2²·2³ = 2⁵).

questions.prompt: How does Snellman handle a quotient of powers with the same base?
choices: A Add the exponents.
B Subtract the denominator’s exponent from the numerator’s: xᵐ/xⁿ = xᵐ⁻ⁿ.
C Multiply the exponents.
D The quotient is always 1.
questions.explain: He defines xᵐ/xⁿ as xᵐ⁻ⁿ by subtracting exponents.

questions.prompt: How does Snellman interpret a negative exponent such as x⁻¹?
choices: A As always equal to −x.
B As the multiplicative inverse: x⁻¹ · x = 1 (e.g., 2⁻¹ = 1/2).
C As undefined for all positive x.
D As the square of x.
questions.explain: x⁻¹ is the multiplicative inverse of x; negative exponents correspond to reciprocals.

questions.prompt: What does Snellman identify fractional exponents of the form x^(1/n) with?
choices: A Only negative integers.
B Roots—e.g., x^(1/2) is the square root of x.
C Logarithms base x.
D The degree of a polynomial.
questions.explain: He connects fractional exponents 1/n to roots; x to the one-half is the square root.
